entries.title: Albania police, protesters clash as thousands rally against the government
entries.summary: Protests are the latest in a long series of antigovernment demonstrations demanding the resignation of PM Edi Rama.
entries.content:
Protests are the latest in a long series of demonstrations demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

Clashes have ⁠broken out between police and protesters in another antigovernment protest in ⁠Albania, this one ⁠called by students and opposition figures to mark the country’s Independence Day.

Albanian police used ⁠water cannon and tear gas on protesters gathered in the capital, Tirana, on Saturday, as demonstrators threw stones and petrol bombs to try to smash street cameras and government building windows.

Video footage showed the main boulevard blanketed in thick smoke as protesters and police exchanged projectiles. The health ministry said eight people were injured, including a police officer and two journalists.

The clashes are the latest in a long series of antigovernment protests in Albania demanding the resignation of Prime ‌Minister Edi Rama.

The leaderless protest movement, which became known as the Flamingo Revolution, began in May with peaceful rallies against a luxury hotel project in a coastal nature reserve linked to United States President Donald Trump’s family.

The project fuelled anger over alleged corruption, as protests expanded in October to include poor healthcare facilities and a lack of prospects for young people.

November 28 is typically a day of national celebrations and a public holiday, as this year marks the 114th anniversary of the country’s declaration of independence.

But this year, thousands gathered in central Tirana as students and opposition parties both called for a nationwide protest.

Police were deployed along the main roads leading in and out of the capital on Saturday, conducting vehicle checks.

“I came here specifically for the protest,” Arian Lleshi, a 33-year-old who travelled to Tirana from the United Kingdom, told The Associated Press. “Why? Because we have been suffering for far too long. We have spread ourselves across Europe and around the world, and it is almost as if we are citizens without a state. We are like stateless citizens.”

The political parties in Albania since the fall of communism in the 1990s “no longer represent anyone,” Lleshi said.

“They need to make way for a new generation of intellectuals and people who have a greater stake in the country’s future.”

Tirana resident Suzana Gjeta, a retiree, told the AP she was demonstrating for both young people and those like herself “who are living on just 120 euros [$131] a month”.

“We hope this system will go, that Edi Rama will go and that this corruption will end,” she said.

In late October, the government gave police the power to temporarily restrict gatherings near public institutions and impose fines on protesters caught looting and concealing their identity. Protests have since drawn smaller crowds.

The European Union, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, has called for an investigation into excessive force by police and called on “all sides to de-escalate the tension”.

entries.title: Iran points to Europe’s war role after Italians killed in Kuwait strike
entries.summary: Italy and Kuwait say an Iranian drone was involved, but Tehran says the US and Israel may be looking to escalate war.
entries.content:
Italy and Kuwait say an Iranian drone was involved, but Tehran says the US and Israel may be looking to escalate the war.

Tehran, Iran – The deaths of two Italians in Kuwait in an alleged Iranian attack could worsen relations between Iran and the European Union, warn experts.

Antonio Saccoccio, 65, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, were working for a European defence company in Kuwait when they were killed in a drone attack on a military site on Thursday.

Iran has officially denied any role in their deaths, calling it a “false flag” operation intended to draw European countries, which have not officially joined the United States and Israel in strikes on Iran, deeper into the conflict.

Riccardo Alcaro, research coordinator and head of the global competition and political risk programme at the Rome-based Istituto Affari Internazionali (IAI), said the reasons why Iran might deny any responsibility for the attack remain unclear.

“Assuming that the drone was launched by an Iraqi pro-Iranian group, the intention would be to degrade Kuwait’s defence capabilities ahead of a possible new confrontation with the US, which Tehran considers very much possible if not likely and hopes it can deter through such actions,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Their insistence on denying responsibility would reflect a dual objective: avoiding being seen as the aggressor while reinforcing the false flag operation narrative, thereby making it easier to challenge the rationale for a possible future US-Israeli attack.”

Divisions

Politically, the deaths could become a sensitive issue in Europe if public opinion starts associating such incidents with the unpopular war launched by the United States and Israel on February 28, crippling energy supplies and driving up prices of gas and petrol worldwide.

Alcaro believes the response from Italy and Europe will be to continue condemning attacks against countries in the region. Countries whose companies operate as contractors at military bases in Kuwait, which has suffered a series of Iranian attacks in recent weeks, will also have to review security protocols for personnel working at sensitive sites, he added.

“Weapon systems, such as the radar that the two Italian nationals were servicing, are highly complex and require continuous technical support, which can probably only be provided by specialised personnel as the case with the Italian Rheinmetall workers shows. This exposes their personnel to these kinds of risks,” he said.

A second narrative coming from state-aligned circles and media in Tehran specifically implicates Ukraine and redirects attention towards Europe’s role in the war – even as Italy and Kuwait accuse Iran.

The deaths follow an attack by Ukraine on two Russian vessels in Libya on Sunday, prompting widespread anger at Kyiv for appearing to drag its war with Moscow into the Middle East theatre.

Foad Izadi, another Tehran-based conservative political commentator, told Al Jazeera that he believes Ukraine was the culprit in a false flag operation.

Izadi, who is an associate professor at the faculty of world studies at the University of Tehran, said European leaders had “the blood of the Iranian people on their hands” for playing a supporting role for US aircraft and operations.

He pointed to statements made by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte that confirmed up to 5,000 US military sorties originated from European bases in support of Operation Epic Fury between February 28 and mid-April.

Approximately 500 US military flights had taken off from bases in Italy in support of the operation, Rutte said in late June. Italy’s Defence Ministry insisted that it had authorised only routine logistical and technical operations, not combat missions.

Relations between Iran and the EU have nosedived in recent years over a range of issues, including Iran’s contentious nuclear programme and regional influence. The bloc has imposed many sanctions on Iran and considers the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a major faction in the Iranian political and military establishment, a “terrorist” organisation.

Izadi said he does not expect relations to improve over the coming years, but said the lingering conflict would only hurt European consumers who are now contending with considerably higher gas and other energy prices for winter.

“It is not to Europe’s benefit to be entangled in prolonged energy wars with Russia or Iran,” he said.

Official response

Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said military installations were targeted in Kuwait and that the deaths of “technicians” maintaining detection antennae for a Skyguard air defence system were caused by intercepted drone shrapnel.

The official response from Iranian authorities has shifted between blame on other actors and denial. Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs was quick to reject responsibility.

“The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war,” wrote Iran’s chief diplomat Abbas Araghchi on X, adding that he called his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts to offer condolences.

Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, Iran’s armed forces spokesman, also issued a stern rejection and said the US and Israel have a history of launching false flag operations to advance their objectives involving Iran. He described the latest accusations against Iran as “a cover for maintaining hostilities and an attempt to increase insecurity in the region”.

State-linked media in Iran also largely reproduced official narratives, including claims of a nefarious covert operation by outside actors.

“False flag during situation of no war, no peace,” wrote the reformist Mardom Salari (rule of the people) newspaper, framing the Kuwait incident within the current precarious status quo.

But some also warned hardline factions in Tehran about the risk of such incidents escalating into all-out war. The state-linked Jomhouri-e Eslami (Islamic Republic) newspaper claimed that the US and Israeli spy agencies were looking for an “excuse” to restart large-scale combat operations against Iran, so Tehran should refrain from launching any preemptive strikes.

“Kuwait’s incident on Thursday showed that the theoreticians who speak and write of the necessity of Iran launching a preemptive attack are playing in the enemy’s court,” the outlet said in an editorial on Saturday, the first day of the week in Iran.

Rome has attributed the attack to Iranian-origin drones, but Foreign Minister Tajani acknowledged the possibility that Iran-aligned militias in other countries could have launched the projectiles. The Italian government has not yet vowed military retaliation, additional sanctions or other punitive measures against Iran.

EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc “must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks” on Kuwait and other regional Arab allies of the EU in order to ensure security for all.

entries.title: Court rejects Argentina’s request to stop UK oil activity near Falklands
entries.summary: An international tribunal refuses Buenos Aires's application, giving the green light to the project off the disputed region.
entries.content:
An international tribunal refuses Buenos Aires’s application, giving green light for the project off the disputed region.

An international court has rejected Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt United Kingdom-authorised oil drilling near the Falkland Islands.

Saturday’s ruling by the United Nations-backed International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea is a setback to Buenos Aires’s latest effort to challenge economic activity around the disputed territory.

Argentina’s request marks the latest spat between the two countries, which fought a brief but bitter 74-day war in 1982 over the UK-administered islands in the South Atlantic.

In September, Argentina launched an arbitration process against London over the Sea Lion project off the Falklands, which is led by the UK’s Rockhopper company and Israel’s Navitas.

Buenos Aires has argued the plan violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute over the sovereignty of the islands is resolved.

It has asked the court to impose emergency measures and order the UK to take the necessary steps “to ensure that no new drilling for exploitation, and no installation of production infrastructure” takes place in the North Malvinas Basin.

It further urged the Hamburg-based court, an independent court set up under UN auspices, to order the UK to “refrain from using the information obtained in the exploration of the natural resources of the disputed maritime areas”.

The Sea Lion oil field is located about 220km (135 miles) from the islands, which lie 600km (372 miles) off Argentina’s Patagonian coast and almost 13,000km (8,077 miles) from the UK.

Argentinian President Javier Milei has doubled down on his country’s claim over the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – since US President Donald Trump said he was open to reviewing Washington’s stance on the territory.

Reacting to the ruling, he said Buenos Aires will continue its efforts to halt the project.

“This decision is not the final word,” Milei said in a statement, noting that Argentina will continue to “assert its rights through all diplomatic, legal and administrative channels at its disposal.”

The Falkland Islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain part of the UK.

But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by the UK after 1833.

London’s argument

The UK, meanwhile, has urged the court to reject the case, saying it was rooted in Argentina’s claims to sovereignty.

London argues the sovereignty claim falls outside the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea’s arbitration process aimed at settling maritime disputes.

The UK government’s chief legal adviser, Ellie Reeves, told the judges in a two-day hearing earlier this month that the order sought by Argentina “would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources, as they are entitled to do so”.

This could have “devastating” economic consequences for the islanders, she said, adding that what Argentina “wants is to take control of those resources for itself”.

Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham also raised the Sea Lion project with Trump in a call in late October.

“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said in a statement.

The tribunal was set up under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which came into force in 1994 and which sets out a “regime of law and order in the world’s oceans and seas, establishing rules governing all uses of the oceans and their resources”.

If the court orders provisional emergency measures, these would be legally binding on both parties.

entries.title: Bootleg alcohol poisonings in Iran see dozens dead and badly injured
entries.summary: A spate of alcohol poisonings in Iran has led to deaths and serious injuries including blindness.
entries.content:
A spate of alcohol poisonings in Iran has led to deaths and serious injuries including blindness.

Two years after four people were executed for distributing contaminated alcoholic beverages – causing the deaths of 17 people and leaving 199 with injuries, including blindness – another spate of mass alcohol poisoning has swept through Iran.

Since mid-November, more than 20 people have died and at least 500 have been poisoned from consuming methanol-contaminated alcohol, the same substance used in medical disinfectants and wound care, and potentially fatal if consumed.

The first death was reported on November 16 in Marvdasht, in Fars Province, central Iran. By Friday, 66 people in Fars Province, 126 in Hormozgan Province in southern Iran, 230 in Razavi Khorasan Province and 15 in West Azerbaijan Province had been poisoned.

Police have launched a crackdown on bootleg alcohol sellers since then and by Friday, about 10 people were arrested across Iran in connection with the cases.

On Friday, the prosecutor of Razavi Khorasan Province said that the poisoning cases in Razavi Khorasan, Fars and Hormozgan provinces were connected. But several individuals had been arrested in connection with a “contaminated alcohol distribution network”.

Banned

A former Tehran police detective, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that any investigation into these incidents will have to look at the wider bootleg alcohol industry to avoid repeat poisoning incidents.

“In cases such as methanol poisoning affecting several cities or provinces, investigators need to look beyond the distribution network and examine the production network as well,” he said.

“Sometimes distributors may not even know that the alcohol they are selling to the public is contaminated. In such cases, investigations usually continue until those responsible for producing the contaminated drinks are identified and apprehended.”

Laws in effect banning alcohol were established in 1980, shortly after the Islamic Revolution, although religious minorities such as Christians and Jews can still access beverages such as wine.

The sale and purchase of alcohol is illegal in Iran, with drinkers potentially facing punishments of 80 lashes and jail, while repeat offenders have been executed.

Despite the strict laws, Hossein Kermanpour, spokesperson for Iran’s Ministry of Health, recently repeated the government’s advice that people should avoid consuming alcohol – but if they do and experience unusual symptoms, they should seek immediate medical attention.

The use of cheap medical-grade alcohol as the base of their products has made the consumption of illicit alcoholic beverages highly risky, the former police detective said.

“They typically buy medical-grade ethanol and mix it with a certain percentage of grape or date-based alcohol before selling it. Some use tea or acorn extracts to alter the colour and taste, while others add tequila or whisky-like flavourings to imitate the taste and appearance of commercial spirits,” he said.

“The problem is that medical alcohol, which is supposed to be ethanol, can sometimes contain traces or higher concentrations of methanol due to various factors. If the ethanol used in production is contaminated with methanol, the resulting product can become extremely toxic. In such cases, even the producers themselves may be unaware that the alcohol they purchased was contaminated, potentially exposing consumers to serious poisoning.”

Medical issues

Iranians say that alcohol is said to be available in major cities, and two official studies conducted in the early 2010s found an increase in alcohol consumption among Iranians aged between 15 and 64.

The National Mental Health Survey commissioned by the Ministry of Health in 2011 estimated that 830 per 100,000 people (approximately 623,000 individuals) had alcohol dependence, while 2,800 per 100,000 were recreational drinkers. A second survey also reported that there was a particular increase in alcohol consumption among people aged under 18 and women. A more recent study by the Ministry of Health in 2021 gave a more mixed assessment about any rise in alcohol use in Iran.

Dr Shadi Hassanzadeh, a general practitioner in Mashhad, told Al Jazeera that only when patients experience extreme medical issues – such as blurred vision, progressive loss of consciousness, and seizures – do they realise this is not ordinary intoxication and seek help, although by then it might be too late to save their eyesight.

“Methanol, or industrial alcohol, is extremely dangerous when used in homemade alcoholic drinks because consumers have no way of detecting its presence. By the time its effects become apparent, serious damage may already have been done to the body,” said Hassanzadeh.

Maryam, a nurse at an ophthalmology hospital in Tehran, told Al Jazeera that despite the law, she does not see people admitted with alcohol-related incidents afraid to reveal consumption of illicit alcohol.

“Since there is a widespread belief that consuming industrial alcohol causes blindness, ophthalmology hospitals are among the first places people turn to for treatment. The most common symptoms they present with are vision problems,” she said.

“Most people do not realise that seeking medical attention soon after consuming industrial alcohol increases their chances of saving their eyesight. Because they often do not know they have been poisoned, they delay seeking treatment until it is too late for doctors to do anything.”

Most cases of alcohol poisoning happen during weekends and national celebrations, she said, when Iranians have a respite from gruelling work and education schedules.

“During the first 24 hours after consuming methanol, the symptoms can resemble those of an ordinary hangover, making it difficult for people to recognise the danger,” she said. “They may only realise something is seriously wrong around 72 hours after consumption, when the symptoms become more severe,” she said.

entries.title: Norse Atlantic ends flights: How Iran war continues to batter aviation
entries.summary: The Norwegian budget carrier is the latest airline to fold under fuel costs driven by the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
entries.content:
The Norwegian budget carrier is the latest airline to fold under ‘eyewatering’ fuel costs driven by the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

The Norwegian airline Norse Atlantic has filed for bankruptcy for its main operating unit, cancelling all flights and halting ticket sales, as soaring jet fuel prices triggered by the United States-Israel war on Iran claim another operator.

The long-haul, low-cost carrier said on Friday that it had failed to secure the short-term financing it needs to keep flying.

It joins a growing list of carriers that have collapsed, entered restructuring or cut routes since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key artery for Gulf oil and refined fuel exports.

Here is what we know.

Why has Norse Atlantic stopped flying?

The board of the airline’s Norwegian operating subsidiary, Norse Atlantic Airways AS, filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court on Friday, after concluding there was “no longer a basis for continued operations”.

The filing came a day after the airline suspended all flights, and two days after it warned that its financial position was “critical”. Its shares closed 85 percent lower on Thursday.

“If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board’s intention to file for bankruptcy,” the company said as it grounded its fleet.

A day later, it confirmed that no rescue had materialised. “Despite extensive efforts, the company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs,” Norse Atlantic ASA said.

“We were unable to absorb the extra cost … Fuel is what toppled this company,” Chief Executive Officer Eivind Roald told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.

The bankruptcy covers only the Norwegian operating unit. Roald said the listed parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, and its UK subsidiary were still trying to find a solution for the remaining parts of the business.

“The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the Company and the Group to find a solution,” Roald said in a statement.

“Many airlines hedge their fuel purchases and stockpile fuel to protect themselves against crises like this. Norse Atlantic did not hedge at all, so it had no protection against rising prices,” aviation analyst John Strickland told Al Jazeera.

As a result, the airline was left fully exposed to spot prices on routes that burn large quantities of fuel.

“Passengers are also unsure about booking flights at a time like this, and the airline faces stiff competition on transatlantic routes,” he said.

Operations at the airline had been shrinking for months. Roald said in May that Norse had cancelled more than 700 flights since the war began and cut 75 jobs that month in a bid to save $50m. It dropped its Los Angeles summer schedule in April and later announced it would pull its New York routes.

The final blow came when the lessors of its Boeing 787 fleet issued termination notices for all of its aircraft, a move Norse is contesting.

“It means Norse Atlantic is unlikely to continue operating because the lessors have terminated those contracts,” Strickland said. “Those lessors want to protect their finances, so if they doubt that Norse Atlantic will pay what it owes, they will terminate the contracts.”

He added that Norse “had favourable contracts before they were terminated”, terms it is unlikely to secure again.

Which other airlines have collapsed or cut back?

The first major casualty after the start of the US-Iran war, which has triggered oil shortages, was Spirit Airlines. The US ultra-low-cost carrier ceased operations on May 2 after talks for a $500m federal rescue failed, citing a spike in fuel prices as a key factor. Spirit, which had filed for bankruptcy twice since 2024, had been flying for 34 years.

“It is with great disappointment that on May 2, 2026, Spirit Airlines started an orderly wind-down of our operations, effective immediately,” the carrier said in a statement.

In Europe, Latvia’s national carrier airBaltic abandoned expansion plans in August and entered Chapter 11 restructuring in the US, citing fuel costs and disruption tied to the Iran war. On October 5, it said it would cut 500 to 700 of its roughly 3,000 jobs and fly a smaller fleet to fewer destinations.

The airline said the redundancies would ensure the “company’s structure and cost base are aligned with the future scale of the carrier”.

In Spain, the Barcelona-based low-cost airline Volotea began formal negotiations with creditors on September 29 under the country’s pre-insolvency procedure. It puts the cost of higher fuel prices since March at about 150 million euros ($174m) and plans to shrink its fleet from 44 aircraft to 30-35, although its flights continue to operate.

“The impact of the war this year will be around 150 million euros, despite everyone’s efforts and decent fuel hedging for the first months,” Volotea’s chief executive told staff, according to the French travel trade outlet TourMaG.

Spanish long-haul carrier Plus Ultra suspended flights to Colombia in June, blaming an “unprecedented increase” in fuel costs. On November 17, it indefinitely suspended its Madrid routes to Buenos Aires and Lima as part of a financial and operational restructuring, leaving Venezuela as its only remaining market.

Larger airlines have also trimmed their networks. United Airlines said in March that it would cut capacity by 5 percent on less profitable routes, while several European carriers, including KLM and Finnair, have extended suspensions of flights to Gulf hubs into 2027.

“The impact has been huge,” Strickland said. “We have already seen a number of bankruptcies, especially among small, privately owned airlines in Europe. We have also seen midsize and regional European carriers struggling and restructuring their debt.”

He warned that the squeeze “will affect the market for low-cost, long-haul flights”.

Why are airlines struggling?

“The main challenge is the fallout from the war involving the United States, Israel and Iran,” Strickland said. “The crisis is affecting oil supplies from the Gulf, and that has driven up the price of fuel.”

Global jet fuel averaged about $99 a barrel on February 27, the day before the war began, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA). It more than doubled to $209 in April. After easing in early summer, prices climbed again, averaging about $190 a barrel in early October and more than $200 in Europe.

The rise is not only for crude. Refineries in the Gulf supplied about one-fifth of the world’s jet fuel and kerosene exports before the war, and disruption to that supply has pushed the “crack spread” – the premium of jet fuel over crude oil – to record levels. As a result, jet fuel has risen in price far faster than oil itself.

The IATA expects the industry’s fuel bill to rise to about $350bn this year from $252bn in 2025, with fuel accounting for 31.4 percent of operating costs, up from about 25 percent. For some low-cost carriers, fuel can account for as much as 60 percent of costs.

It forecasts that global airline profits will halve to $23bn, with net margins of just 2 percent.

“War-related disruptions in the Middle East and rising fuel costs have shifted the outlook for airlines to the worse,” IATA Director General Willie Walsh said when the forecast was released in June.

IATA’s chief economist, Marie Owens Thomsen, said: “This is eye-watering stuff,” according to Aviation Week. “It will affect absolutely everyone in the global economy.”

Airlines have passed part of the extra cost on to travellers. US airfares were 23.4 percent higher in August than a year earlier, and the five biggest US carriers earned 18 percent more passenger revenue in the third quarter even as traffic grew by less than 1 percent.

“Even when airlines hedge against crises like this, the higher costs will still be passed on to passengers,” Strickland said.

Budget long-haul carriers are the most exposed, however, because their customers will not pay much more for a ticket. “They depend on price-sensitive travellers, and with fuel costing more, they haven’t been able to sell many seats at prices that work for them,” Strickland said.

“They don’t have the same market power as Qatar Airways and other carriers,” he added.

How have Middle East airlines fared?

They were hit hardest by the start of the US-Israel war on Iran at first. Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad all halted operations during the most intense, earlier phase of the war, and have flown reduced schedules since.

The damage shows in the numbers. Emirates reported a 68 percent drop in half-year profits before tax to $1bn for the six months to September 30, with capacity down 17 percent and passenger traffic down 25 percent.

But the Gulf carriers have remained profitable while others have failed, and several factors are now working in their favour.

Their first advantage is having fuel on their doorstep. Emirates, Qatar Airways, Etihad and Saudia operate close to some of the world’s largest refining centres and, with Gulf refiners unable to export normally, local stocks have grown. Qatar’s reserve cover has risen by more than five months and the UAE’s by about 15 days, according to Bloomberg.

Gulf governments are also working to cut their exposure to the strait. Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, the UAE minister of state for foreign trade, said he expected a plan to reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, particularly for oil, to zero by the end of this year, the Emirati daily Emarat Al Youm reported.

While still much more expensive than before the war, jet fuel is cheaper in the region than in the rest of the world. In early October, jet fuel averaged about $165 a barrel in the Middle East, compared with more than $200 in Europe, IATA data shows.

The Gulf carriers also have deeper pockets and better protection than airlines like Norse. Emirates’ fuel costs before hedging rose 60 percent, but $1.9bn in hedging gains cut the net rise to 13 percent, and the region’s big airlines entered the crisis with large cash reserves to absorb the rest.

Competition has thinned, too. Many foreign airlines have stayed away from Gulf airports, with Finnair suspending flights to Dubai and Doha until March 27, 2027, and KLM’s Dubai service suspended until March 2027. That leaves more of the market to home carriers.

Strickland pointed to that market power as the key difference between Gulf carriers such as Qatar Airways and budget operators such as Norse, which have had to compete on price alone.

The advantage has limits, however. Qatar Airways has trimmed its departures by about 7 percent for the northern winter schedule, and the Gulf carriers remain exposed to any renewed fighting in the region.

What is the outlook for 2027?

Airline executives expect little relief.

Panellists at an IATA energy forum this month warned that jet fuel prices could spike again in 2027 as inventories shrink and spare refining capacity remains limited.

Some airlines are testing whether they could withstand $200-a-barrel jet fuel in 2027, according to the Reuters news agency.

Raising fares has limits. “Fares are really determined by demand rather than the cost inputs,” Oliver Wyman consultant Scott Laurence told Reuters, warning about the risks of deeper capacity cuts.

Many are heading into next year less protected. Ryanair has hedged only about 25 percent of its fuel for the year from April 2027, and Turkish Airlines just 12 percent. Air France-KLM is modelling a 2027 fuel bill, after hedging, of 10.4 billion euros ($12bn), up from 9.2 billion euros this year.

Airlines are also wary of locking in today’s prices. “The risk is that oil prices might roll off and we catch ourselves on the wrong side of the market,” Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary told analysts this month.

That points to higher fares and further capacity cuts, particularly on marginal routes.

entries.title: Taiwan opposition party wins re-election in Taipei mayoral race
entries.summary: Voters across Taiwan have cast ballots for mayors, council members and other local leaders.
entries.content:
Voters across Taiwan have cast ballots for mayors, council members and other local leaders.

The candidate for Taiwan’s opposition Kuomintang party (KMT) has secured re-election in the mayoral race for the capital, Taipei, after his main rival conceded defeat.

Voters on Saturday cast ballots for some 11,000 positions across Taiwan’s 16 counties and “six municipalities”, or largest cities, in local elections closely watched by China, which considers the self-ruling island to be a part of its territory and has pledged reunification by force if necessary.

The DPP looked set to clinch half of the municipalities, taking back Taichung – the island’s second most populous city – along with Tainan and Kaohsiung.

But its Taipei candidate, academic Puma Shen, conceded defeat late on Saturday to incumbent Chiang Wan-an of the KMT. Chiang won by a double-digit margin in the previous election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate.

In addition to the capital, the KMT is likely to win the other two municipalities: New Taipei City, the most populous of the six municipalities, and Taoyuan.

Election campaigns ahead of the vote centred on domestic issues including transport, childcare and the environment, rather than disputed ties with China.

The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the ruling DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims. KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April.

Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defence said 33 Chinese warplanes encircled Taiwan on Friday, including bombers and fighter jets, along with eight warships.

The KMT dominated the last local elections, winning across 14 cities and counties. The DPP managed only 5, while other parties and independents took 3.

Preparations and campaigns for the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections are expected to start after Saturday’s election results.

President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP is likely to run again, while outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen could be the KMT’s frontrunner.
